drills.q: How many general-purpose registers does x86-64 have?
drills.why: Eight inherited from the 8086 and eight added by AMD64. That number is the constraint every optimisation above this layer is working against.

drills.q: After mov rax, -1 then mov eax, 5, what does rax hold?
options: 5, because writing a 32-bit name zero-extends into the full 64 bits
0xFFFFFFFF00000005, because only the low 32 bits were written
drills.why: Measured. Set rax to all ones, write through eax, shift right by 32 and the result is zero. A 32-bit write clears the upper half.

drills.q: After mov rax, -1 then mov ax, 5, is the upper half of rax cleared?
options: No. A 16-bit write leaves the other 48 bits exactly as they were
Yes, the same rule applies to every narrow write
Yes, but only on processors newer than 2010
drills.why: This asymmetry is the whole trap. The 16-bit and 8-bit forms had to keep behaving the way 16-bit code from 1985 expected, so the partial-register dependency survives in exactly the widths nobody writes on purpose.

drills.q: Why does a 32-bit write clear the upper half at all?
options: It removes the dependency on the register's previous value, so the
It is an accident of the 8086 encoding
drills.why: If the write preserved the upper bits, the new value of rax would depend on the old one, and the processor could not start the instruction until whatever last wrote rax had finished.

drills.q: Why do compilers emit xor eax, eax rather than mov rax, 0?
options: It is shorter to encode, and the processor recognises it as producing a
To clear the flags at the same time
drills.why: It is idiom recognition rather than arithmetic. The same reasoning is why you see it everywhere in optimised output and almost nowhere in source.

drills.q: Which way does the stack grow on x86-64?
options: Downward on Linux and upward on Windows
drills.why: It is a layout decision rather than a truth about stacks. The stack starts high and the heap starts low so the two can grow toward each other without either having to know in advance how much room the other needs.

drills.q: After push a then push b, where is a?
drills.why: b was pushed last so it is on top, at [rsp]. Because the stack grows down, the item below the top is at a higher address, which reads backwards the first several times.

drills.q: By how much does one push change rsp?
options: It depends on the width of the operand
drills.why: Measured: take rsp, push once, and subtract. push is sub rsp, 8 followed by a store, and pop is a load followed by add rsp, 8. There is no stack in the hardware, only a register and an agreement.

drills.q: In what order do the first six integer arguments go?
options: Left to right on the stack
drills.why: This is the System V AMD64 convention, and it is not guessable from the register names. Beyond six, arguments go on the stack.

drills.q: Why does the Linux syscall interface use r10 where a function call uses rcx?
options: The syscall instruction overwrites rcx with the return address
r10 is faster to access from ring 0
Historical accident with no reason behind it
drills.why: The hardware takes rcx for its own purposes the moment syscall executes, so the kernel interface cannot use it for an argument. This is the kind of detail that bites you exactly once.

drills.q: Which of these must a function preserve for its caller?
options: None; the caller saves everything it cares about
drills.why: Those are the callee-saved half. Everything else, including all the argument registers and rax, may be destroyed freely by a called function.

drills.q: Why split the registers into callee-saved and caller-saved at all?
options: Either rule alone is wasteful, and splitting lets a compiler pay only for
To leave room for future registers
drills.why: If everything were callee-saved, a leaf function using two registers would still preserve sixteen. If everything were caller-saved, every call site would spill everything live.

options: Writing past the end of the stack
Keeping a value in memory because there is no free register for it
Losing a value when a called function clobbers a register
drills.why: With sixteen registers and more live values than that, something has to live in memory and be moved back and forth. It is the most common reason compiled output is slower than you expected.

drills.q: In a program with no C runtime, where does execution begin?
options: At the first instruction in the file
At whichever label is declared first
drills.why: main is a libc idea: the runtime sets things up and then calls it. Without a runtime the kernel jumps straight to the entry symbol, which is _start by default.

drills.q: Why can a program with no C runtime not end with ret?
options: Nothing called it, so the value ret pops is not a return address
ret is not a valid instruction at the entry point
It works, but leaks the process
drills.why: There is no caller and no return address. The program has to ask the kernel to end it, which is syscall 60 with the status in rdi.
